body:
Arguments are difficult because somewhere within almost every argument are two people who believe they are right. The disagreement may be about almost anything—a broken promise, an expectation, a favor, an act that caused hurt, something we needed and didn't receive, a difference in belief, or simply an emotion the other person does not understand.

Then Jesus says something rather severe in today's Gospel: “You hypocrite! Remove the wooden beam from your eye first; then you will see clearly to remove the splinter in your brother's eye.” The word *hypocrite* caught my attention. Jesus doesn't seem particularly gentle here. But perhaps even more interesting is what he says next. Jesus does not tell us there is no splinter in our brother's eye, nor does he tell us to ignore it. He tells us to remove the beam from our own eye **first**. Then we can see clearly.

Maybe there is an extraordinary lesson about conflict hidden within those few words. Before deciding exactly what another person has done wrong, perhaps we are being asked to examine ourselves as part of the conflict. What have I contributed? Was it my expectation, my pride, my anger, my words, my assumptions? Did I fail to listen? Am I responding to what actually happened, or am I responding to the hurt it caused me? This doesn't mean the other person was right. Removing the beam from our own eye does not make the splinter in theirs disappear. Perhaps it simply allows us to finally see it clearly.

And then maybe we can determine what love actually requires. Sometimes that may be forgiveness. Sometimes an honest conversation. Sometimes acknowledging our own fault. Sometimes exposing something that truly needs to be brought into the light. And sometimes it may mean ending the argument altogether so that conflict does not continue producing more conflict. Because sin can beget sin. Someone hurts us and we respond in anger. Our anger hurts them. They become defensive and respond harshly. We judge their response, they judge ours, and soon neither person is dealing with the original problem anymore. Hurt has produced hurt, judgment has produced judgment, and anger has produced anger.

Not every argument is sinful. Disagreement is part of being human. But what we do within that disagreement can take us somewhere very different. And that leaves me with a harder question: **What is the truth?** We naturally assume that what we see is the truth, but our vision can become clouded by disappointment, fear, pride, resentment, previous experiences, and our desire to be understood. The other person's vision may be clouded too. Perhaps conflict is sometimes two people reacting strongly to something neither one can see completely clearly in that moment.

Maybe that is why Jesus tells me to begin with my own eye. Not because I am necessarily the one who is wrong, not because another person's behavior should be excused, and not because truth doesn't matter, but because **I am the only person whose beam I can actually remove.** I can examine my behavior. I can take ownership of my words. I can question my assumptions. I can recognize where pride or hurt has distorted my vision, and I can stop contributing to an endless cycle of retaliation.

Perhaps after doing that, I may discover that I was wrong. Or I may discover that I was right about what happened but wrong in how I responded to it. Maybe I will see that both of us contributed something. And sometimes, after removing the beam, I may see that the splinter really is there and something needs to be said. But now I can approach it differently—not simply to prove that I was right, but to see clearly enough to help remove what is hurting us.

I am not entirely sure this is everything Jesus intended when he spoke these words. But I do know that conflict, in its countless forms, has followed humanity from the beginning. Perhaps Jesus is showing us one way to stop it: **before reaching for the splinter, look for the beam.**
prayer: Lord, when conflict clouds my vision, give me the courage to look first within myself. Show me what belongs to me—my pride, my anger, my assumptions, my words and my faults. Help me take responsibility for them without ignoring what is true. Then give me clear eyes to see the other person with mercy and wisdom. When something needs to be said, let me speak it in love. When something needs to be forgiven, help me forgive. And when conflict begins creating more conflict, give me the humility to stop the cycle. Amen.
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
title: Who are the enemies?
